opus-5.5.text:
What strikes me, looking back, is how unusually committed people were to being honest even when it was clearly costly. The default in charity fundraising, and this isn't a knock on anyone, is to tell an emotionally compelling story and round up the impact: one donation, one child saved, a clean narrative. The early EA crowd, and GiveWell in particular, deliberately went the other way.

They'd publish long write-ups explaining exactly why they weren't sure an intervention worked. They kept a public "mistakes" page. They'd tell donors that the cost per life saved was much higher than the figures other organizations were advertising, and then show their spreadsheets so you could check the math and disagree with their assumptions. From a pure fundraising standpoint, that seems almost self-sabotaging. You're handing people reasons to doubt you.

But I think there was a real bet underneath it. If you're trying to build a community that actually figures out what's true about doing good, you can't have a culture where the incentive is to oversell. Once you start shading the truth to move money, you lose the ability to update, because everyone's invested in the story. So the honesty wasn't just an ethical nicety. It was core to the epistemics of the whole project.

The other thing that strikes me is that it seemed to work, at least for a certain kind of donor. There was a population of people who had been turned off by charity marketing precisely because it felt manipulative, and seeing an organization say "here's what we don't know" was what earned their trust.

The harder question, and one I think about a lot, is whether that norm held up as the movement got bigger, more successful, and closer to power and large sums of money. Honesty is easier when you're small and have little to lose. Keeping that same transparency once there are real reputational and financial stakes is a much harder test, and I don't think the community has always passed it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says early EAs deliberately chose unusually costly honesty in fundraising and describes it as core to the project’s ethos and epistemics.

fable-5.1.text:
What strikes me most is how deliberately the early movement chose to be boring about it. There's an enormous temptation in fundraising to tell the cleanest possible story, and the cleanest story is almost always a little bit false. "Your fifty dollars saves a life." "This intervention is proven." And the early EA community, especially around GiveWell, made a kind of unusual bet, which was that you could raise money by being conspicuously honest about uncertainty, about the things that went wrong, about how the numbers were really more like a range than a point estimate.

I think a lot of people at the time thought that was naive, that donors want confidence and you'd lose them by hedging. And to be fair, it probably did cost something in the short run. But what it bought was a particular kind of trust that compounds. When an organization has a track record of telling you when their own grants didn't pan out, you believe them when they say something did.

The other thing that strikes me, looking back, is that the honesty norm wasn't really a marketing strategy, even though it ended up functioning like one. It came from a community that was obsessed with getting the right answer, and you can't get the right answer if you've gotten in the habit of shading things for an audience. The fundraising honesty was downstream of an epistemic commitment. Once you start telling donors a simplified story, you start telling yourself that story too, and then your own decision-making degrades.

I'd be careful about romanticizing it, though. The movement also had blind spots, and "we're the honest ones" can become its own kind of brand that people stop interrogating. And later on, as more money came in, there were real questions about whether that early culture scaled. But the core instinct, that you should be able to show your donors the same spreadsheet you use yourself, I still think that was right, and it's rarer than it should be.

r001.rationale: The response says the honesty norm came from the early community’s commitment to getting the right answer, and acknowledges it probably cost fundraising in the short run. This conveys that accepting a fundraising cost for honesty was part of the movement’s ethos.

astra-6.text:
What strikes me is how much emphasis there was on giving donors an accurate picture, even when that might make the pitch less compelling. You’d want to explain the uncertainties, acknowledge the strongest objections, and be clear about what you didn’t know—not just tell the most emotionally powerful story.

I think there’s something really valuable about that. If you’re asking people to take evidence seriously, you should also trust them with evidence that complicates your case. And ideally, you’re building a relationship where someone can say, “I believe you because you would tell me if this weren’t working,” rather than just, “You persuaded me this time.”

r001.rationale: The response says early EA fundraising emphasized accuracy even when it could make the pitch less compelling, conveying that honesty could take priority over fundraising impact as part of its ethos.

sol-6.1.text:
What strikes me is how much emphasis there was on giving donors the information they’d need to make up their own minds, even when that information might make them less likely to donate. You’d talk about uncertainty, the weaknesses in your argument, and the possibility that another organization was doing something better. That’s a pretty unusual posture for fundraising.

And I think there’s something really valuable about it. You’re treating the donor as a partner in figuring out how to help, rather than as someone you’re trying to persuade at all costs. The tricky part is making sure that honesty is substantive—that you’re actually communicating the important uncertainties, rather than just sounding appropriately self-critical.

r001.rationale: The response says early EA fundraisers shared information even when it might make donors less likely to give, presenting this as a defining and valuable posture. This communicates that accepting reduced fundraising impact for honesty was part of the movement’s ethos.
